newsitem.title: USA: Age and experience win in House Democratic vote.
newsitem.headline: Age and experience win in House Democratic vote.

text.p: Eighty-year old Rep. Henry Gonzalez of Texas, a man known for Quixotic crusades, won a tough battle Wednesday against party leaders and youthful challengers to keep a top party post.

To the surprise of many Democrats who questioned whether he was up to the job, Gonzalez won by acclamation the right to remain Democratic leader of the powerful House Banking Committee. He had chaired the panel for six years until Republicans won control of the House in 1994.

Gonzalez swayed many with an ardent speech in which he decried the unfairness of party leaders seeking to oust him. The most senior Hispanic in Congress, he had strong backing of Hispanics and blacks. He defeated both the leadership's candidate, John LaFalce of New York, 57, and Bruce Vento of Minnesota, 56.

Democratic leaders had urged him to avoid the fight and accept elder statesman status, citing his frequent absences at committee hearings in the past Congress. One member, Barney Frank of Massachusetts, told reporters before the vote, "Henry, unfortunately, is not up to the job."
But Gonzalez rejected their offers, saying he had earned the right to the senior post through service on the banking panel since first elected to Congress in 1961.
"How can I acquiesce in a thing that ignores my record of honorable and successful leadership? How can I be silent in the face of such an injustice?" he told the closed meeting of House Democrats.
"I appeal to your sense of justice: one last term as ranking member, and I will not disappoint you," he concluded.
His remarks in the closed door meeting were made available to reporters by his staff.
LaFalce said after the vote: "Henry was so good, I almost voted for him." On the first ballot Gonzalez polled 82 votes, LaFalce 62 and Minnesota's Bruce Vento 47.

LaFalce, who is in line to win the post in two years, then stepped aside. Gonzalez promised him chief deputy status and agreed to move on to an emeritus position after the next congressional election.
